The main challenge lies in the nonlocal nature and multiterm structure of these kernels. Second-order models, derived from first-order ones with help of the stick-slip model for heat transfer, offer an alternative for engineering applications. Notably, these second-order models can be interpreted physically and mathematically. The kernels in such models represent memory effects or stick-slip processes, making them applicable to diverse problems, like heat conduction with insulating surfaces and thermoelectric phenomena. The nonlocality of these kernels implies spatial correlation between heat flux components. The second-order model's coefficients also influence this correlation, indicating insulating effects to be significant. The low spatial correlation coherence length is a characteristic trait of superconducting materials. The coherence length in our model emerges as a function of the coefficients in the nonlocal kernel. The low coherence length can also be achieved in very dense semiconductor materials. The heat transport behavior in metals, exhibiting a finite coherence length, can also be modeled. The thermal conductivity coefficient serves as a measure of the coherence length in these materials. The coefficients in the nonlocal kernel are directly proportional to this length. The models presented are verified using both analytical and numerical approaches. The stick-slip process is validated by comparing the model with other established methods. The results show good agreement between the two methods.

Literature can be broadly classified into two main categories based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. These intermediate cues are then solved for in the second stage, a process that is often facilitated by Projection-based methods. However, two-stage pipelines have the drawback of requiring ground truth data that matches the problem at hand, a constraint that can be quite restrictive in practice. To address this limitation, we propose a Projection-based approach that operates in a single stage, a technique we call Single-Shot Projection-based Network (SSPNet). SSPNet directly estimates a 6D object pose without the need for ground truth data or intermediate cues, a capability that sets it apart from two-stage pipelines. Furthermore, SSPNet is grounded in the optimization of a robust function that aligns projections of object keypoints with observed image keypoints. To facilitate efficient optimization, we transform the problem into a low-dimensional one, a process that involves regularization of the rotation component. Experimental results demonstrate that SSPNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various datasets, a performance that is further confirmed by ablation studies. Additionally, SSPNet is distinguished by its ability to generalize well to novel scenarios, a trait that is partly due to its single-shot setup and partly due to the robust function that it employs.

This new formulation was shown to accurately calculate wave propagation speeds in one-dimensional, homogeneous solids, which matches the classical elasticity theory.  Additionally, it was able to capture the onset and growth of cracks in brittle materials, providing a seamless modeling approach.  Furthermore, it was applied to the simulation of impact damage in heterogeneous materials, where it accurately captured stress and damage at various impact strengths.  Ultimately, this new formulation offers a reliable method for peridynamic simulations of impact, damage, and fracture in diverse materials.  It has the potential to be extended to more complex materials and scenarios, such as nonlinear fracture, and three-dimensional material systems.  It is also possible that it can be applied in multi-physics frameworks that combine peridynamics with other methods like finite elements.  This new formulation provides a strong foundation for the modeling and simulation of material discontinuities in the future.  It has been validated through one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional numerical studies, which demonstrate its ability to accurately capture fracture and damage phenomena

The proposed bound itself has theoretical value, and we show that it meets the fundamental requirements for a QFI metric. Specifically, this bound serves as a generalized QFI metric for subnormalized states and extends the traditional QFI in this context. The proposed bound uses a generalized fidelity applied to a truncated state, which is derived from the m largest eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors of the probe quantum state ρθ. By focusing on families of unitary exact states, we examine the properties of the introduced lower bound and demonstrate its practical utility for efficiently estimating the QFI. Moreover, we discovered that the critical factor influencing the tightness of this lower bound is the spectral distribution of ρθ. By comparing different families of unitary exact states, we determined that the uniformly distributed states offer the most stringent lower bound. The introduced near-term quantum device applicable lower bound of QFI is a significant advancement towards achieving precise quantum metrology using near-term quantum devices. Since direct measurement of RSSI is subject to noise, we employ a technique known as indirect RSSI estimation. To counteract interference, only non-overlapping channels are utilized for signal measurement. A Gaussian Mixture Model is used to construct the probability distribution of estimated RSSI and a Bayesian approach is applied to determine the maximum likelihood estimate of location. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method achieves a level of accuracy comparable to that of a location finding method previously introduced by our research team, known as LFD. Furthermore, we found that the accuracy of location finding is largely unaffected by levels of interference. However, it is noticeably improved when there is no interference. Over a grid-based surface with 64 sections, the average error rate for location finding in both scenarios of interference present or absent is less than 1 meter. A corresponding average error rate of less than 0.5 meter is achieved for a surface divided into 256 sections. To further validate our research, a comparison of the proposed method with location finding techniques other than LFD is also included. A corresponding paper has been submitted for publication in the Journal of Communications. Additionally, the source code for the simulation is publicly accessible on GitHub. Based on this research, an open-source tool for simulating wireless sensor networks is also being developed, known as Simuloze.

Neural Networks (DNNs) via reverse analysis involves identifying the most influential middle-layer (feature extractor) that contributes to the final output. However, due to the complex nature of DNNs, directly backtracking input data to middle-layer activation patterns is highly non-deterministic and non-traceable. To address this challenge, we present a novel framework, FEAT. This framework utilizes two main components. Firstly, it uses a surrogate model, constructed from training data, to predict activation patterns based on input data. Secondly, it determines the required input data to produce a specific activation pattern in the feature extractor layer through optimization. FEAT is then capable of reverse analyzing the provenance of DNN outputs by backtracking from the feature extractor layer to the input layer. We evaluate FEAT using three platforms - CloudRaj, CloudFlow and XCAT2012 - in scenarios of malicious trojan attack and quantitative analysis, respectively. The results demonstrate that FEAT successfully identifies the most compromised feature extractor layer in trojan attacks and accurately determines the input data required to trigger a specific activation pattern in the feature extractor layer. This is a significant achievement as this information was previously inaccessible. FEAT is now capable of quantitatively analyzing the provenance of DNN outputs. We anticipate that FEAT will significantly contribute to advancing the provenance analysis of DNNs, particularly in detecting malicious backdoors, and will be of substantial value to the security and reliability communities. Kalman-Bucy initially illustrated that minimum variance estimation has a duality link to a linear quadratic optimal control problem, which also provided a concrete method for deriving the Kalman filter from the optimal control solution. Building upon Kalman-Bucy's findings, this work expands on this relationship by generalizing it to nonlinear systems, specifically those governed by continuous-time Markov processes with nonlinear, noise-affected observations. In doing so, it presents a new stochastic process that enables the translation of the minimum variance estimation problem into an optimal control problem, which is then solved via the maximum principle to derive the equation of the nonlinear filter, ultimately revealing Kalman-Bucy's filter as a specific solution for linear systems. Furthermore, the proposed approach's ability to handle general nonlinear systems makes it a more versatile method. In addition, the mathematical framework generated can be applied to extend the duality between estimation and control to other, related problems. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory. This connection offers a novel interpretation of cut-elimination as a geometric algebraic process. Building on this framework, we explore a new type of semantics for proof nets and investigate the solvability of specific instances, including finite proof nets and proof nets with a bounded cut depth. The MaRF framework consists of several key components. 

1. Multi-Baseline Stereo: This component uses a combination of stereo matching techniques to generate point clouds from pairs of images. Each pair is analyzed using a parallel baseline approach, one horizontal and the other vertical. This yields two sets of 3D data points per image pair, with the x and y coordinates corresponding to the stereo matching results and the z coordinate calculated using the image spacing or camera parameters.

2. Geometric Matching: This component uses multi-view geometric matching to merge the point clouds generated by stereo matching. Each 3D data point is assigned an unique identifier, along with a set of vectors representing the observation history. These vectors help calculate the geometric matching cost, with the optimal matching result used to merge the point clouds

The problem of minimal supervision in image recognition is a pressing issue, as it necessitates the reduction of human intervention in the training process. One of the key limitations of existing methods is their reliance on a large amount of unlabeled data and the quality of pseudo-labels generated during the training process.

To address this issue, a novel self-training technique called Bi-training has been developed. By splitting the model into two parts and training them alternately with labeled and pseudo-labeled images, Bi-training reduces the discrepancy in the feature space, thereby improving the accuracy of pseudo-labels and the recognition performance. Through comprehensive experiments, the efficacy of Bi-training has been demonstrated on three large-scale dataset benchmarks, namely ImageNet, CIFAR100, and Stanford Stanford Car, under three different unsupervised learning protocols. Notably, Bi-training outperforms the current state-of-the-art approaches by a significant margin of 5.3%, 4.3%, and 9.3% respectively, in terms of top-1 accuracy.

To further enhance the Bi-training method, an automatic label assignment protocol has been developed to determine the confidence threshold of pseudo-labels based on the nearest neighbor distance between samples. By eliminating noisy pseudo-labels resulting from the intermediate feature space, this protocol improves the accuracy of pseudo-labels and, ultimately, the recognition performance.

These event sequences are generated by various processes such as network traffic, stock market transactions, and medical diagnoses. A crucial goal in mining these event sequences is to identify patterns that hold significant meaning, yet this is hindered by the varying lengths of sequences and their disparate representations. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this claim is difficult to gather. The treatment duration is impacted by various unmeasurable patient factors and coincides with the admission decision, which are challenging variables to manipulate. As such, conventional causal studies are impractical to conduct. By utilizing a dynamic Bayesian network representing the admission process over time, we were able to model patient flow through the ED and estimate average response curves. Our results show that prolonging the treatment duration leads to a later arrival of patients and a decrease in admitted patients, but does not alter treatment completion times or admission rates. In contrast, starting the admission process earlier than standard practice results in an increased proportion of patients being admitted and a more uniform arrival time for treated patients. Furthermore, accelerating the admission process for some patients comes at the expense of delayed admissions due to the altered patient flow. Our findings suggest that optimizing the standard treatment duration and admission timeline may hold significant potential for improving Emergency Department admissions. As this study relies on observational data and simulations, it does not imply causality; rather, it suggests that varying critical process times has notable effects on Emergency Department patient flow. an intriguing connection where increased educational attainment tends to exacerbate income disparity. The Mincer equation's nonlinear relationship between wages and education, along with the variability in its return on investment, appear to play crucial roles in this occurrence. A combined approach of least-squares and quantile regression analysis has been developed to disentangle these contributing factors. The new methodology relies on the functional derivative method and is subsequently applied to examine the case of Argentina from 1992 to 2015. Our investigation reveals significant variability in the return on investment for education and a wage growth profile that increases up to a high school level, followed by diminishing returns at higher levels of education. The analysis also demonstrates that the distribution of education completion levels is skewed, with a significant portion of the population holding lower levels of education. Combining these findings, we assert that the 'paradox of progress' in Argentina can be attributed to the intersection of two processes: one that amplifies income disparity through variable returns to education and another that exacerbates inequality by virtue of the education distribution's right skewness, leading to a delayed attainment of maximum wage potential by individuals with higher levels of education. In contrast, countries like Chile and the United States present different scenarios, where the return on education investment remains constant and their education distribution is centered, respectively. Our study suggests that educational systems should prioritize providing access to higher levels of education while also focusing on bridging the existing knowledge gaps in fields that exhibit steady returns to education investment. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement labeled nodes with high-confidence pseudo-nodes. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling approaches have several issues: they are based on an oversimplified assumption that neighboring nodes share similar labels, leading to incorrect pseudo-nodes being generated; they rely on a predetermined threshold to categorize nodes into different classes, resulting in poor performance due to the difficulty of setting this threshold; and they only utilize local information, overlooking the global structure of the graph. To address these challenges, we propose a novel pseudo-labeling approach called Self-training with Node Embedding Structure Awareness, which incorporates the semi-supervised pseudo-labeling problem into a self-training framework. By leveraging the structural features encoded in node embeddings, our approach effectively eliminates pseudo-nodes with incorrect labels, optimizes pseudo-nodes' label categories through an improved clustering method, and integrates graph structure into the pseudo-labeling process. Consequently, our approach outperforms existing pseudo-labeling approaches and non-pseudo-labeling baselines on six datasets, with an average increase of 6.5% accuracy and 3.4% F1-score. Notably, our approach exhibits remarkable growth in pseudo-label quality and node embeddings' accuracy as the number of labeled nodes decreases. The research demonstrates that edge magnetic impurities can induce novel localised states and unconventional transport phenomena in graphene's edges and sublattice bonds.

law that objects in circular orbits remain in elliptical orbits has been derived using basic principles. The approach is similar to past derivations in utilizing conservation laws to determine an equation for an orbit. In this instance, trigonometry is employed to derive the comparison equation for an ellipse, without invoking calculus. The derived equation compares the compared the radius of an orbit at a specific point with the distances from the focus point in an orbit. In this derivation, conservation of angular momentum leads to the comparison equation for an orbit (θ = ωt), and conservation of energy leads to the equation for a planet's energy, which is then used to define a constant (E0). By setting angular momentum equal to a constant (h), and energy equal to a constant (E0), the equation for an orbit is defined as r^2 = (a^2)b, where 'a' is a constant representing the semi-major axis, and 'b' is a constant representing the distance from the focus point. By comparing this equation for an orbit with the equation for an ellipse, r^2 = e^2 + b^2, where 'e' is a constant representing the eccentricity of an orbit, the eccentricity of an orbit can be determined as a function of 'b'. DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 1024 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes.

Recent research indicates that ensembles have distinct benefits, particularly in uncertainty assessment and adaptability to dataset changes. This study demonstrates the limitations of these benefits, revealing that a single larger model can achieve similar outcomes. Firstly, ensembles lose their superiority in uncertainty assessment because a larger model can learn more complex models of uncertainty. Secondly, ensemble flexibility stems from the diversity of individual models, but a larger model can be designed to have greater diversity through techniques like model mixing. Lastly, dataset shift can be addressed in ensemble methods, but a single larger model can also be trained to be more robust to distribution changes. Overall, while ensembles offer various advantages, these benefits can be replicated by a larger, more complex model. This research suggests reevaluating the premise that ensembles are preferable to single models. Rather, the focus should be on what makes these models effective: adaptability, diversity, and the ability to model uncertainty. By incorporating these attributes into a larger model, its performance can approach that of an ensemble. This approach could lead to breakthroughs in understanding and achieving these attributes within machine learning. This research is a initial step in exploring this attribute paradigm and the resulting implications. Further study is needed to fully understand this concept and its applications. This study examines how GAN training is affected by high-frequency components.
During the typical GAN training process, significant high-frequency differences compel the discriminator to excessively focus on high-frequency features.

Consequently, EPR did not effectively challenge the underlying theory of quantum mechanics. The source of EPR's paradoxical conclusion that QM is incomplete stems from a misapplication of von Neumann's projection postulate to measurements with degenerate spectra, a misuse of the axiomatic framework of quantum mechanics. Subsequent attempts by Bell and Clauser-Horne to reinterpret EPR as challenges to either the physicality or independence of the vector space representing states in QM, as well as to the underlying logic of QM, were unsuccessful. It is demonstrated that EPR's key conclusion can be derived from a combination of von Neumann's projection postulate and the principles of classical logic, rendering the EPR argument obsolete. Moreover, EPR's conclusion that QM is incomplete can be replaced by the conclusion that von Neumann's projection postulate is incompatible with the principles of classical logic. The resulting complete and consistent reformulation of quantum mechanics, known as classical QM, has been consistently applied to various foundational and practical issues in quantum mechanics, as well as to the underlying theories of relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory. Classical QM has served as the foundational theory of relativistic quantum mechanics and has been successfully used to resolve the relativistic epr experiment and the problem of relativistic quantum equilibrium, and has also been applied to the quantum measurement problem

In order to gain insights, we examined a disk surrounding a ~1 Myr old low-mass star using data that combined spectral energy distributions and high angular resolution continuum maps. This led to the determination of inner and outer disk radii, dust mass and a characterization of the planetarity of the system. In the case of the detected submillimeter source, it was found to be consistent with a thermal dust model, indicating that it is likely a disk fragment rather than a star-forming region. Furthermore, the analysis suggested that the system may have entered the stage of planetary formation if we assume a typical proto-planetary disk mass, indicating that core formation could have occurred when the gas surrounding the star was still present. However, if we consider the mass of the disk's gas component as measured, the system would have a higher mass ratio of core to surrounding material. It is also possible that the system's mass is the result of a disk that has lost a significant portion of its gas component through winds or a massive planet has formed and led to a reduction in the gas component's mass. Based on the detected properties, it is likely that the process of planetary core formation from dusty solid material in proto-planetary disks starts early in the star's evolution and continues for an extended period. It is also possible that the formation of planets from dusty solid material is restricted to a limited time frame compared to gas accretion.

Furthermore, the method allows for analog computation in a single layer, resulting in substantial time savings and lower energy consumption compared to digital computation. Traditional quantum teleportation employs two classical bits but relies on the sender having a single copy of the transmitted qubit. Our investigation explores the possibility of reducing the required classical information if the sender has access to multiple qubit copies without restrictions on their states. To that end, a modified quantum teleportation method has been devised that allows resetting the shared entanglement using local operations, thereby allowing the transmission of less than two classical bits, specifically, one bit more than half the time, on average. The Art Composition Attributes Network (ACAN) was trained by integrating domain expertise from art criticism and assessing its impact on CycleGAN-based apple-to-orange image transformations. My findings reveal that CycleGAN outputs benefit from composition consistency when constrained by ACAN, but this constraint also impairs the model's ability to capture underlying semantic features. Consequently, I explore two approaches to strike a balance between composition principles and semantic features in CycleGAN. CycleGAN+ACAN was evaluated against baseline CycleGAN models with and without composition constraints, as well as a configuration using an iterative training strategy to optimize both generator networks simultaneously. My analysis demonstrate that all three methods suffer from compromised performance due to the composition constraint. To address this, I propose an unsupervised approach that combines CycleGAN and ACAN, involving an iterative training protocol aimed at thoroughly learning both artistic composition and semantic features. To accomplish this, I integrated an additional objective function based on composition principles, along with activation regularization, trained alternately multiple times. The resulting model demonstrated improved performance compared to baseline CycleGAN models with and without composition constraints. To validate the efficacy of my approach, I performed an ablation study examining the impact of training frequency on the model's performance. My findings indicate that increasing the training frequency enhances the model's ability to learn from the composition constraint without hindering its ability to capture semantic features.

implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the first step is to convert input data into a probability distribution and a cost function. The OT operation is then performed between the probability distribution and the mean pooling probability distribution. By dissecting the dual problem of the OT, a dual UOTP layer can be defined and implemented. Through experiments on different tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and graph classification, the proposed UOTP layers have achieved superior performance compared to conventional global pooling layers. Furthermore, the flexibility of our unbalanced optimal transport theory-based framework enables novel global pooling designs to be created. One such example is the Signed Pooling layer, which has also demonstrated better performance than conventional global pooling layers. However, traditional machine learning methods face challenges due to the imbalance of ECG and patient data, resulting in biased outcomes. Ultimately, this study highlights the need for further research in this area, suggesting potential avenues for future investigation. -Carlo Planning (POMCP) efficiently creates approximate policies for large complex decision-making scenarios where some information is unavailable. This tree search algorithm operates by creating a probabilistic tree of potential future states and their associated probabilities based on the given observations and a pre-trained policy. This system then uses a heuristic function to guide the search downward in the tree, typically optimizing expected outcomes. After a predetermined depth is reached in the tree, POMCP collects all possible paths back to the root node and averages their associated values, also incorporating a cutoff for computational efficiency. 

POMCP has seen significant use in both robotics and AI research due to its speed and flexibility, particularly in practical applications such as the learning of navigation and mapping skills. This system has been used to train agents for a variety of tasks such as planning a trajectory, managing movement, and decision-making, among others. 

In our research, we challenge POMCP to a competition against other planning algorithms and find that it no longer performs optimally in all scenarios. This discovery motivates us to create a more efficient variant of POMCP, which we call "Stochastic Partially Observable Monte-Carlo Planning" (SPOMC), using ideas from randomized optimization. This new algorithm incorporates a more sophisticated method of expanding the tree that includes a more effective heuristic function, which has been shown to reduce computational costs while still maintaining approximate policy accuracy. 

Our experiments reveal that SPOMC outperforms POMCP in terms of solution quality

It has been discovered that these boulders are most densely packed in higher northern latitudes, specifically between 10-20 degrees north of the equator. When comparing the distribution of larger boulders (> 105 m), it is evident that those in the northern latitudes contain more massive objects than their corresponding southern counterparts. Moreover, boulders in the northern latitudes show a more uniform distribution of larger objects, transitioning from a steep power-law spectrum to a gentler slope as the object size increases. It is hypothesized that this difference arises from the erosion of boulders due to Ceres's surface C-rich material, which would result in varying degrees of degradation based on the local water activity levels. If this theory holds true, it implies that Ceres's surface water activity is more pronounced in the northern latitudes. It has also been discovered that boulders in Ceres's center are less massive than those found elsewhere, which could be attributed to the same degradative processes. Ultimately, these findings highlight the significance of Ceres's surface water activity and its impact on the planet's boulder distribution, while also shedding more light on the characteristics of Ceres's surface composition. This surge in digital usage by children necessitates a corresponding rise in cyber safety awareness among them.
Children are now exposed to the digital world from a young age through devices such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops, which they use both at school and at home.
As a result, they are more likely to come across cyber threats in their daily lives, underscoring the need for enhanced cyber safety measures.
Given the significance of this issue, various countries have introduced comprehensive programs in schools to educate children about cyber safety.
However, there remains a scarcity of localized programs, particularly in developing countries, which could effectively address the unique challenges posed by diverse cultural contexts.
To bridge this gap, we have developed an extensive program that caters to the specific needs of schoolchildren in Malaysia, which has a multi-ethnic population.
Through our cyber safety program, we aimed to raise awareness among schoolchildren about potential threats, promote safe online behaviors, and empower them with problem-solving skills to navigate complex cyber situations.

We investigate how well a simplified, economically rational model predicts the observed consumer behavior, with the model assuming uniform preferences among consumers. The key factors that determine model accuracy in this context are (1) whether a single equilibrium exists in the market and (2) whether the public plan is dominant among these equilibria. With limited information about consumer preferences, we use an empirical approach to estimate the distribution of consumer types from actual behavior data. Our approach also enables the calculation of optimal water conservation policy metrics, including total conserved water and consumer welfare gains. To mitigate this issue, gradual verification has been proposed, integrating static and dynamic checks to accommodate partial, complete, or absent specifications. Although it has been extended to static recursion, gradual verification has a significant drawback: the inability to confidently vouch for program safety when specifications are incomplete. To address this limitation, we present gradual verification for recursive data structures, allowing the use of partial specifications, but also include an innovative method to formally certify program safety even when specifications are incomplete. Our technique leverages denotational semantics to define a partial correctness notion applicable across a broad spectrum of programming languages. Furthermore, we outline an approach to implement this notion through a hybrid reasoning engine, combining static and dynamic checks. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we have developed a prototype in the functional language Forseti. Our technique does not necessitate a specific evaluation order, dynamic type checking, or other complex features, as it can incorporate existing specification methods and a straightforward, top-down evaluation order. Our implementation demonstrates that gradual verification for recursive data structures can be feasible even with simple specification methods. Moreover, we have formally verified that our implementation preserves the defined partial correctness property. Our technique is versatile, as the same methods can be applied to various programming languages with recursive data structures. Acting as selective barriers, membranes isolate cells due to the challenge ions face in traversing their dielectric shielding. In place of an outdated condition lacking dielectric properties, we introduce a new mathematical description that models a cell membrane with a lipid bilayer, embedded with channels allowing ions to pass selectively. This setting seeks to solve the linearized Poisson--Boltzmann--Laplace equation in the presence of dielectric inhomogeneities to find the electrostatic potential, and with it, the ion distribution, channel gating mechanisms, and the associated flow. Due to the inhomogeneities and the new channels, the analysis is computationally demanding, and we propose a novel strategy using a specially adapted finite element method. Through a series of numerical experiments, we demonstrate the ability of the new model to capture the intricate interactions between the membrane's dielectric properties, ions, and channels, revealing novel insights into its behavior. This groundbreaking mathematical description and analysis pave the way for a comprehensive understanding of biological processes at the nanoscale. To facilitate simulations in complex cellular environments, we also introduce an open-source software tool. This high-performance computational approach, built on adaptive finite elements, enables rapid calculations even in high-dimensional spaces. With its domain-specific optimization, the software now allows for efficient simulations of biological systems. This paper documents the software, sharing its source code, and reports on a preliminary set of numerical results.

To address this gap, we introduce the "STAX" model, a novel data-driven approach that utilizes large-scale trip data to model the public transportation network. the development of Private Deep Learning (PDL). PDL employs differential privacy to safeguard both machine learning models and their training processes. Despite improvements, PDL remains far behind its traditional counterpart in terms of accuracy. This paper challenges PDL's fundamental assumption that learning models must remain private even after they've been trained, deeming this constraint unnecessary. A new approach, called Relative Privacy, emerges as an alternative. Relative Privacy protects the data only during the training process, releasing model parameters anonymously. Our proposal, called Privately Trained Deep Learning with Relative Privacy (PTDRL-RP), enhances PDL's accuracy and efficiency. PTDRL-RP-RP achieves this by making the model parameters public, thus eliminating the need for differential privacy. To maintain data protection, PTDRL-RP employs a novel dual-optimization approach. Experimental results show that PTDRL-RP outperforms PDL significantly in both accuracy and efficiency. This work is the first to introduce Relative Privacy as an alternative to differential privacy in PDL, presenting PTDRL-RP as a more effective solution. PTDRL-RP also opens doors for future research in Relative Privacy and data protection. Additionally, the code used in this study is available at https://github.com/leonardo-c/PTDRL-RP.

This method involves using the knowledge gained from a complex, powerful model (the teacher) to train a simpler model (the student). To achieve this, a novel multi-task knowledge distillation framework has been developed, allowing existing ITS/AD models to train AD models from scratch while leveraging the knowledge gained from these models. This framework's effectiveness has been demonstrated in various cross-task and cross-model training scenarios, outperforming traditional supervised training methods. Furthermore, experiments have shown that by combining multiple knowledge distillations processes, the accuracy of AD models can be further enhanced. To validate the framework's practicality, a real-world demonstration has been conducted using two specific models. Moreover, a new human-AI collaboration score is introduced that synthesizes the perspectives of humans and AI on interaction dynamics. To demonstrate the versatility of the HALIE framework, an extensive study covering different interaction contexts (either creative or problem-solving) and human-AI collaboration levels (ranging from non-existent to mutual collaboration) is conducted, providing significant insights. The framework, along with the accompanying resources, are made available to the public at halie.io. Two additional papers - "Human-AI Collaboration in Conversation: A Meta-Analysis" and "Evaluating the Quality of Human-AI Collaboration" - provide supplementary analysis and methods. A particular type of symmetry breaking known as nematicity, characterized by ground-state degeneracy due to an arbitrary symmetry being broken, has gained significant attention in the study of electronic systems.  Nematicity can arise from symmetry breaking caused by either orbital repulsion or electron-electron interactions and can significantly affect electronic properties by creating an anisotropic ground state. A comprehensive understanding of the nematicity's influence on electronic properties and possible signs of its presence will be discussed here. highly driven thermal convection is a key phenomenon.
The ultimate balance between thermal flux and velocity was previously proposed for this highly driven thermal flow.
Despite ongoing experimental and numerical investigations, direct observation of this critical regime remains unattained so far.
We now demonstrate that the ultimate state of this highly driven thermal flow is achievable once the heat diffusion layer becomes completely isolated from the flow resistance and exists solely within the turbulent core.
The thermal flux may then significantly increase by one order of magnitude due to this separation.
The findings from our study present robust evidence that the ultimate state of this highly driven thermal flow occurs when the heat diffusion layer is fully immersed in the turbulent core.
This is a highly likely occurrence in many natural convective systems on Earth.
The separation of thermal diffusion from the overall flow resistance then significantly decreases the heat transfer efficiency by one order of magnitude, which is a highly probable occurrence in these systems.
The ultimate state of this highly driven thermal flow is also influenced by the geometry of the system and can be attained in channels as well as in systems with an infinite number of layers.

A popular sampling approach involves manipulating pathway branches to increase the capture of low-probability segments, yet accurately categorizing reaction configurations often requires a backward or forward look at timeline data. 
We propose an efficient solution to overcome this issue by employing basic data structures and provide a clear demonstration of this strategy using non-equilibrium umbrella sampling (NEUS), which may be applied to other techniques to extract transition path theory statistics. 
NEUS is particularly useful for capturing coarse grained reactions since it does not require a complete pathway and can be combined with other techniques like coarse graining to explore rare events. 
NEUS involves placing energy barriers along the reaction pathway and is capable of providing free energy surfaces at the equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. 
By applying NEUS to a simple reaction, we demonstrate that it can accurately calculate free energy surfaces even when equilibrium conditions are reached. 
NEUS also provides an equilibrium distribution that can be used to calculate reaction rates and other important reaction statistics. 
A major advantage of NEUS is its ability to handle reactions with multiple pathways by segregating different pathways and applying energy barriers independently. 
NEUS is capable of being extended to more complex reactions by incorporating additional factors like energy barriers and non-equilibrium conditions.

we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation in the desired characteristics. To accomplish this, we have formulated two types of artificial vocal qualities. The first, comprising the extreme versions of the acoustic characteristics (very warm or very competent), led to the synthetic voices being perceived as unnatural and non-human. Conversely, the moderate versions of these attributes (somewhat warm or somewhat competent) contributed to the development of synthetic voices that were perceived as being voiced by humans. We posited that the extreme versions of the acoustic characteristics (very warm or very competent) resulted in the synthetic voices exceeding the bounds of the physical world in terms of spectral density, thereby making them inhuman. We then attempted to rectify this issue by mixing the moderate versions of the acoustic characteristics with other parameters. Interestingly, this led to a significant improvement in the perception of the synthetic voices as being voiced by humans, even when the additional parameters were randomly generated. Our study underscores the importance of regulating the attributes of the synthetic voices to fall within the bounds of the physical world in order to improve their human-like quality. Moreover, our research highlights the utility of the acoustic characteristics in understanding the complex factors underlying synthetic speech perception. Finally, our study demonstrates the value of the synthetic voice attribute manipulation in enhancing their human-like quality. Our findings have far-reaching implications for the development of synthetic speech in applications such as customer service, navigation, and educational tools.

Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT. In our study, we examined how LITT affects this brain region by creating detailed maps of the treated area before and after LITT. These maps were compared to each other by a computer system to assess how much the treatment changed the brain. Additionally, we tracked how LITT evolved over time by looking at high-resolution videos of the treatment. Our results showed significant changes to the treated area after LITT. These changes were also observed in other parts of the brain. Our study found that combining two computer systems to analyze the treatment was more accurate than using either of them alone. Our research showed that LITT changes the treated area in different ways depending on the shape of the treating laser. Our work laid the ground for how to use computer systems to analyze the treatment based on how LITT is given. Moreover, we found that using a special shape to give the treatment led to better outcomes. Our study demonstrated that detailed brain maps can be used to help give the treatment based on individual brain patterns. Furthermore, we successfully tested our computer system on a large dataset of 85 LITT treatments. Our work showed that detailed brain maps can help evaluate the effectiveness of LITT more accurately. Ultimately, our research may improve how LITT is given and how its effects are evaluated, leading to better seizure control and quality

Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results with minimal training data. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of using deep learning techniques on rFS, and evaluate the performance of several convolutional neural network architectures. The anticipated outcome of this research will enable the development of a universal and adaptable weather detection system that is not limited to a particular environment and can identify multiple weather conditions. The rFS dataset and corresponding source code are available online at the specified URLs. Additionally, a pre-trained model and classification code can be found at these URLs. In the case of pre-trained encoders such as BERT, specific vulnerabilities arise from the LayerNorm's scaling factors and biases. We identify these anomalies as 'norm-gates', effectively acting as a bottleneck that concentrationally amplifies the impact of pruned weights. According to our research, these norm-gates can cause a 10 times greater decline in performance compared to expected predictions from the remaining weights. To mitigate this issue, we have devised two strategies: 1) scaling-norm invariant regularization and 2) zero-init pruning-invariant pre-training. Both approaches have led to successful results in enhancing the robustness of pruned BERT models against various types of pruning. Our research findings offer practical insights into understanding and addressing the problem of pruning-induced performance degradation. Medical dataset annotation for use in training data-hungry deep learning models is costly and time-consuming. Leveraging information from clinical practices, such as medical records or measurements, can greatly reduce these costs. However, precise lesion identification using automated processes is complex. Our work quantitatively assesses how bounding box coordinate noise influences Faster R-CNN object detection networks' performance for detecting breast masses. To simulate various degrees of noise, we altered the size of the bounding boxes, increasing them by as much as six times the original dimensions. This experiment was conducted using the well-maintained CBIS-DDSM collection of mammography data. Our results indicate that noise propagation during training reduces the network's accuracy in distinguishing lesions from background due to an imperfect correlation between the true location and the network's proposed bounding boxes. Furthermore, we found that using the standard Intersection over Union criterion led to a decline of up to 9% in the area under the FROC curve. To counter this effect, we suggest using the Soft Jaccard criterion to optimize the object detection network's training. This method can tolerate some bounding box coordinate noise and does not require precise matches between the true and predicted annotations. Our results demonstrate that using the Soft Jaccard criterion reduced the decline in the area under the FROC curve by as much as 5%. Our work's source code and trained models are publicly available on GitHub

Our research introduces a novel technique, known as dynamic efficiency enhancement (DEE), to expedite the QKD process without compromising its security. By dynamically adjusting the efficiency of efficient source modules based on real-time computational outcomes, DEE enables faster QKD generation without the need for continuous source activation. This innovative approach is largely influenced by classical computing's dynamic circuit switching models. Our source modules in the DEE scheme comprise two main components: an activation source module and an efficiency source module. The activation source module triggers source activation based on the computational outcome, while the efficiency source module adjusts the source efficiency accordingly. Our DEE model accelerates the QKD generation without altering the security-related computational complexity, thereby making it compatible with cutting-edge algorithms. Our experiments have demonstrated that DEE can boost QKD generation speed by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude compared to conventional efficient source schemes. To gain a better understanding of this behavior, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the knowledge acquisition process of language models when provided with in-context prompts. Our investigation employed a novel training approach inspired by the observational learning paradigm from animal cognition studies. The results show that language models are capable of efficiently learning from in-context prompts and can achieve comparable performance to that of specialized models trained end-to-end for specific tasks. Additionally, we found that these models can automatically identify the relation between the prompt, the context, and the task, and that they can learn to perform more complex tasks by combining multiple simpler prompts. Importantly, the observed learning abilities are found to be robust across different model architectures, tasks, and language models, and are independent of the size of the context snippets. Ultimately, the findings of our study highlight the remarkable ability of language models to acquire new knowledge quickly and flexibly in response to changing in-context prompts. At the same time, the observed abilities also raise fundamental questions about the nature of the knowledge representations and the types of processes involved in language model learning. To answer these questions, we propose a comprehensive theoretical framework that views language model training as a form of regularized learning that balances the extraction of general knowledge from distributed representations and the acquisition of task-specific knowledge from the training data. The proposed theory is closely related to the idea of observational learning but is unique in that it is applicable to language learning as well.

These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. By adapting zones to handle the continuous time dimension in a symbolic manner, our work offers a new approach to the timing domain. This involves defining suitable'metric zones' that encompass'metric regions' - the continuous counterparts of metric intervals - and developing algorithms to operate within them efficiently. Through this, we demonstrate that (i) the timed domain can be handled in a symbolic manner; (ii) the standard operations for combining metric temporal logic specifications can be performed in a way that exploits metric zones; (iii) the resulting'metric monitor' operates in an online manner; (iv) the method extends the standard 'wait-and-decide' approach with a 'wait-and-show-decisions-so-far' strategy that enables earlier decisive verdicts; and (v) the method also addresses the problem of ambiguous timing, again enabling earlier decisive verdicts. Although this strategy works well for continuous data storage, it's not the most efficient option when files are large and modifications are occasional, resulting in excessive bandwidth and storage usage. A new algorithm has been developed to efficiently manage data with lower priority files using a single, updated copy of the files, stored at each location, which is then replicated across all other storage locations only when changes occur. A study comparing the two approaches on the Grid's nine-tier storage hierarchy showed that the single-copy method significantly reduces bandwidth usage up to 80%, and also demonstrates improved storage efficiency, up to a 35% increase, in certain scenarios. A flexible and adaptable system has been implemented that allows the prioritization of data depending on specific user needs, and also incorporates an automatic failover system to ensure seamless data recovery. A demonstration of the single-copy method's effectiveness is presented, along with an examination of its implications on data recovery and a detailed analysis of its performance on various storage tiers and data sizes. A comparison of the two strategies's effects on bandwidth and storage usage is provided, and a discussion on the potential pitfalls and limitations of the single-copy method is included. compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The geometric properties of this module determine various properties of the original partial differential operator, such as its ellipticity, smoothness, and polynomiality. The study of these properties is known as the global inverse problem. The global inverse problem was partially solved for elliptic differential operators in a recent study. This study further extends these findings to differential operators with symbols that are merely polynomial outside of a certain singular set. The study establishes a complete solution to the global inverse problem for these operators by accounting for their singular behavior. The key concept here is a new notion of a 'connection,' which is introduced as a tool to study such problematic operators. The study reveals that a crucial aspect in resolving the global inverse problem is not only the properties of the operator itself but also the properties of the differential module it defines. Based on this realization, a broad class of singular operators with elliptic, smooth, and polynomial properties on a manifold are identified, and their compatibility operators are explicitly defined. The study also demonstrates that these compatibility operators are unique and concludes with a broad generalization of the global inverse problem

individual model prediction variability has been extensively documented. Despite ensembles providing confidence in prediction precision, they also amplify a novel risk factor for adversarial attacks. We term this phenomenon "confidence amplification." This phenomenon suggests that ensembles are both more precise and more vulnerable to attacks than individual models.

We have developed a theoretical framework that helps estimate the impact of confidence amplification. This framework comprises three key components: 
1. An attack amplification theorem, which demonstrates how ensemble structure affects adversarial attacks.
2. A quantitative model of confidence amplification, which links ensemble structure to prediction precision and adversarial tolerance.
3. An algorithm for optimizing adversarial attacks within this framework.

Our empirical analysis of various machine learning models reveals that ensemble structure significantly contributes to adversarial tolerance. Notably, novel adversarial examples induced in ensembles are also effective against individual models, while utility-preserving attacks also demonstrate amplified effects. Moreover, models utilizing probabilistic predictions exhibit greater confidence amplification and adversarial tolerance. We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/alex-alex-alex/EnsembleConfidenceAmplification. 

This research signifies a significant milestone in understanding adversarial robustness, as it establishes a theoretical foundation for quantifying and mitigating confidence amplification. It also offers practical guidance for optimizing adversarial attacks within this framework. Furthermore, it sheds light on the relationship between prediction confidence and robustness, as well as the potential of ensemble structure to affect adversarial tolerance.

Model checking, a method within formal verification, faces challenges in coping with the enormity of modern system specifications. This difficulty stems from the exponential explosion problem, which makes fully checking all possible system states infeasible. Despite this limitation, model checking remains a valuable approach, especially when used in conjunction with targeted property-directed exploration. This leads to the utilization of directed exploration techniques, such as directed model checking, which focuses property verification rather than comprehensive system validation. This study delves into the effectiveness of directed model checking by applying it to two real-world safety-critical systems: the Linux IP Spoofing and BitBANG network interface. The investigation evaluates its practicality as a replacement for traditional model checking. The findings demonstrate that directed model checking can be a more efficient alternative, capable of detecting safety violations in a more efficient manner than traditional model checking. This efficiency makes directed model checking a viable choice, especially when combined with other optimization strategies. The findings provide insights into the practical application of directed model checking in industry-standard safety-critical systems. The model checking tool used in this study is KeYForJava, an advanced, full-fledged verification tool capable of formal verification. The investigation highlights the capabilities of directed model checking as a effective system validation approach. The experiential evidence from this study suggests the incorporation of directed model checking in safety-critical system development

A range of methods has been used to mitigate data movement costs, including the use of cache hierarchies, aggressive prefetchers, and more recently, near-data processing, where some processing occurs close to the memory.  However, these techniques have limitations and often lead to inefficient resource allocation, particularly when data movement is critical or not feasible.  To address this, we introduce a new approach, memory-access driven near-data processing, which integrates a memory controller with a near-data processor.  This allows for more flexible resource allocation and better handling of data movements.  We evaluate different architectures and show that our approach leads to significant improvements in energy efficiency, scalability, and reliability.  Additionally, we explore various application scenarios and find that our model optimizes resource allocation, resulting in improved performance and lower costs.  We further demonstrate the practical feasibility of our design by estimating the area, power consumption, and memory access latency of the near-data processor.  This research provides a foundation for future work on memory-access driven near-data processing. -driven methods have gained significant traction for their ability to analyze vast datasets, identifying intricate long-range relationships in complex quantum systems. Although neural networks excel at extracting patterns from data, their quantum applications require careful consideration of parameters and architectures to prevent overfitting. Furthermore, quantum phenomena often manifest through rare events, rendering traditional machine learning less effective. To address these limitations, researchers are developing new, quantum-inspired models. This study employs a quantum game of spin models, where Ising model and Perceptron model compete for dominance. By simulating these models on classical and quantum hardware, researchers evaluate their performance using the Ising model's lowest energy state and analytical solutions. Our findings demonstrate that quantum models outperform their classical counterparts across all simulation times, even when the difference is only noticeable at very low temperatures, indicating a potential for improvement of up to two orders of magnitude in certain conditions. Additionally, our analysis suggests that the degree of parameter optimization can be reduced by up to 13.5 times without compromising model efficiency. These initial results indicate significant potential for AI-driven quantum simulations to surpass their classical counterparts in modeling spin models. Moreover, the success of these quantum models despite only being able to access rare low-energy states challenges our current understanding of the trade-offs between quantum and classical learning and may point to the benefits of using deeper neural networks. Lastly, our study paves the way for future experiments on the quantum hardware of IBM Quantum Experience devices, enabling direct comparisons between classical and quantum models of spin interactions.

Device-to-Device (D2D) communication holds the potential for substantial enhancements in energy efficiency, network capacity, and data transfer rates. However, the increasing number of active devices in D2D networks raises concerns about their individual access to the wireless medium and the potential for excessive device transmission. To address these challenges, this research focuses on developing dynamic transmission strategies that minimize the overall energy consumption of D2D users while maximizing their data transfer rates and managing device transmissions for optimal access to the wireless medium. To achieve these goals, the study introduces two novel transmission strategies: the D2D Wake-Sleep strategy and the Power-Control strategy - each offering distinct objectives and a range of optimization techniques - and evaluates their performance using a multi-layer optimization framework that accounts for different levels of network optimization. Through simulation-based analysis, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of these strategies in achieving optimal performance and presents a comprehensive comparison of the proposed methods. Simulation results show that the D2D Wake-Sleep strategy outperforms the Power-Control strategy, particularly in terms of individual device energy efficiency. Furthermore, the study presents three levels of network optimization - macro, micro, and nano scales - each addressing distinct network design challenges and presenting a novel approach for D2D optimization. To facilitate evaluation of these concepts, the study introduces a simulation tool that enables accurate modeling of complex D2D networks and their performance under different transmission strategies. Overall, this research presents an essential foundation for optimizing D2D communications in 5G networks

Nevertheless, these methods may fall short in situations where the navigation task has multiple feasible solutions or the environment's layout can be confidently determined through sensors. In response, an algorithm called RGG* has been developed. It generates a navigation route in the form of a reduced convex hull from a set of geographically relevant key points. However, since these identifiers contain sensitive information, such as personal identifiable data, the record linkage process needs to be carried out with confidentiality considerations in place. This requirement is known as privacy-preserving record linkage (PPRL) and has led researchers to explore the application of differential privacy and efficient encoding methods like Bloom filter encoding to ensure linkages are made anonymously. While the standard differential privacy approach addresses privacy concerns effectively, it overlooks other significant factors like unfair linking biases. To address this gap, a new framework is proposed, combining the benefits of variational Gaussian mixture models (VGMMs) and the application of differential privacy and fair data encoding methods. This new framework allows for the creation of fair linking encodings that not only ensure personal data remains anonymous but also accommodate individuals equally during the linkage process. Experimental evaluations conducted on various real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework produces accurate linkages, outperforming existing PPRL techniques in terms of fairness. This new framework is expected to contribute significantly to the development of privacy-preserving record linkage techniques. Additionally, a Python package offering these innovations is available for public use through the spgroup GitHub repository. The emission spectrum in the red to near infra-red range from AT2017gfo could be adequately explained as the outcome of kilonova effects; nonetheless, no consensus emerged on the causes behind the blue light emission prevailing at the onset (approximately the initial 1.5 days). This discrepancy led to two primary theories being considered: radiance originating from a component lacking lanthanides or a shock wave interaction resulting in a cocoon-like emission. To investigate the possibility of distinguishing between these hypotheses, researchers simulated similar light curve scenarios, employing Bayesian analysis. The results indicate that an ultra-violet satellite capable of rapid follow-up observations after the gravitational wave detection, such as the James Webb Space Telescope with a time frame of approximately 0.25 to 0.5 hours following GW170817, would have enabled the differentiation of the two processes. Moreover, similar light curve scenarios have been applied to the recent event AT2019pad, and these findings suggest that the late-time ultraviolet emission might be the result of a cocoon-like emission. This implies that a similar late-time ultraviolet emission was present in GW170817 and that a swift follow-up observation in the ultra-violet range could offer crucial insights into the binary merger event. The proposed ultra-violet observational strategy is also recommended

To overcome this, we introduce a new approach called CGradAlign, which first transforms a complex image into a simpler form, and then uses PGradAlign to identify target areas. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test code. The research analyzed the perspectives of developers from six open-source projects, inquiring about the influence test smells have on test code and whether they consider it a pressing concern. The results indicate that while developers often view test smells as minor concerns for their own code, they recognize the potential for test smells to negatively affect the overall test code quality. Notably, this study reveals two key findings. Firstly, developers may not always consider test smells in their test code, suggesting a need for more awareness about test smells. Secondly, developers may not necessarily agree with the classification of test smells as bad smells, indicating a need for a more nuanced approach to test smells. The research recommends developers to prioritize test smell removal in their test code and encourage developers to participate in discussions regarding the classification of test smells. Moreover, this study recommends developers to reflect on the implications of test smells

Cryptocurrency and transactions can be facilitated through "smart-contracts" coded in a specific programming language with predictable outcomes. In this study, a method for formally modeling blockchain-based transactions was presented along with a tool, called FairSim, capable of accurately simulating the interactions between multiple contracts, including cases where interactions are not programmed explicitly. and their counterparts play a vital role in achieving goals and guiding optimization. However, these tools face practical and theoretical limitations when it comes to handling complex objectives. For instance, formulating a utility function becomes impractical when the objective involves navigating a high-dimensional space that is difficult to describe. Moreover, even when a utility function is available, its optimization can be both theoretically and computationally challenging. As a solution, other objectives such as risk and reward are sometimes used but they come with their own set of limitations. Ultimately, these problems have sparked the development of goal-oriented optimization methods that learn the objective itself, often represented as a utility function, risk, or reward, through interaction. One such method, called objective discovery, has the potential to simplify the formulation and optimization of complex objectives, and we believe it has numerous applications across various domains including AI, economics, and psychology. However, a fundamental question arises - can we design an objective discovery method that consistently produces a beneficial objective? Based on our analysis, we found a crucial requirement for objective discovery methods to avoid negative outcomes and found that this need has significant theoretical implications. We used this framework to evaluate the capabilities of objective discovery methods and found that existing methods are limited in their ability to produce beneficial objectives. To address this limitation, we proposed a new objective discovery method called Beneficial Objective Discovery and found it to be both efficient and effective. We tested our method in both theory and practice and found it to produce superior results compared to other objective discovery methods

(2020) for Reinforced Vickrey-Clarke-Young model, we derive optimal incentive schemes when there are multiple platform choices and network effects are present. A key finding is the development of a dynamic programming approach to find the optimal incentive schemes. Given that one platform can dictate the probability and fee of user matching, we use stochastic control theory to formulate optimal strategies. We validate the existence of these optimal policies through numerical analysis and show that having monopoly power enables better control over user matching, thus yielding higher revenue. However, this monopoly power also makes the platform more vulnerable to attacks from colluding users. Our research offers insights into the critical design parameters of the Reinforced Vickrey-Clarke-Young model, such as the impact of user valuation distribution and fee of charge. We have developed a novel numerical solution to this complex optimization problem. Our investigation into the dual-role platform, acting both as a platform and a user, reveals that under specific conditions, the optimal strategy is for the platform to behave like a user when its probability is less than a certain threshold. A crucial condition is that the dual-role platform must use the fee of charge by the other platform as the discount factor in a certain Markov process. Our analysis also demonstrates that having a dual-role platform generally yields higher revenue than having a monopoly power, although the latter can better protect the platform from user collusions. Our research offers new perspectives on the design of incentive schemes in the Vickrey-Clarke-Young model.

a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while assisting with various development tasks.  Over time, the digital assistant becomes not only a useful tool but also a sophisticated system for decision-making, emulating the expertise and problem-solving strategies of the human professional it interacts with.  The course explores how to design and implement intelligent systems that harmoniously combine the unique strengths and capabilities of humans and machines.  The course syllabus outlines 10 lecture topics and includes associated readings, as well as a list of recommended references, and supplementary material.  A related set of additional files provides additional insights and resources.  Specifically, Appendix A describes in more detail the digital assistant's architecture, Appendix B presents a more comprehensive review of relevant research areas, and Appendix C includes supplementary material relevant to Lecture 3.  Additionally, a related technical report is available for further information.  The course website with additional resources is located at https://stanford.io/2F4NaO.
